claimTextExcerpt: Helicopter take-offs and landings at aerodromes may not be restricted to designated runways or landing areas.
At aerodromes with an air traffic control service, all helicopter movements are subject to the permission of the ATC unit.
When helicopters land or take-off on the manoeuvring area within sight of the VCR, the terms 'CLEARED TO LAND' or 'CLEARED FOR TAKE-OFF' followed by the position shall be used.

When helicopters land or take-off at locations not on the manoeuvring area, not in sight of the VCR, or unlit at night, the phrase 'LAND AT YOUR DISCRETION' or 'TAKE-OFF AT YOUR DISCRETION' shall be used.

Relevant traffic information on other aircraft (airborne or on the ground) shall also be passed when authorising helicopter movements at locations not on the manoeuvring area, not in sight of the VCR, or unlit at night.
The name of the designated landing/departure point/area should be stated when authorising helicopter movements at locations not on the manoeuvring area, not in sight of the VCR, or unlit at night.
The term 'TOUCH DOWN' shall be used to describe an aircraft coming into contact with the surface in accordance with normal operation.
A clearance to land leaves the pilot of a helicopter free to either enter a low hover, or to touch down, as appropriate.
The use of 'taxi' indicates the pilot is free to air taxi or ground taxi at his/her discretion.
For take-off from the apron (or location not on the Manoeuvring Area) for a Direct Departure, the phrase 'Take-off at your discretion' shall be used.
When vehicles are operating in close proximity to aircraft, drivers should be extremely vigilant and comply with Rule 42/43 of the Rules of the Air and, if applicable, ATC instructions.
Correct RTF operating technique must be observed by all users.
For all vehicles on the movement area, a continuous listening watch must be maintained to be aware of movements and intended movements of other traffic.
Air/Ground Communication Service operators are not to pass instructions and must use the phraseology they would use for the movement of aircraft on the aerodrome.
Drivers on first call should state the ground station they are calling, identify themselves by their vehicle call sign and state their position and intended destination.
Where the planned route includes crossing a runway, this should be included in the initial call.
If a controller replies 'standby', the driver shall not proceed until permission is given.
If a controller replies 'hold position', the driver shall not proceed until the controller calls back with permission.
If the defined point in a clearance is not the intended destination, drivers must stop at this point and further permission shall be requested.
The controller/FISO may include the instruction 'hold short' to reinforce the point beyond which the vehicle may not proceed.
Requests for pushback or powerback are made to ATC depending on the local procedures.
Taxi instructions issued by a controller will always contain a clearance limit.
The clearance limit is the point at which the aircraft must stop, unless further permission to proceed is given.
For departing aircraft, the clearance limit will normally be the holding point of the runway in use.
Taxi clearances should, wherever possible, be noted down by pilots.
POB (total persons on board) may be added, e.g. where a flight plan is not required and has not been filed.
Instruction to report vacated may be omitted when aerodrome control has continuous sight; 'Air-taxi' may be used for fixed-wing/helicopters.
Permission to proceed on the apron may include instructions to ensure safe operations.
Drivers should note carefully the position to which they may proceed, particularly where the intended route involves crossing a runway.
Under no circumstances shall a driver cross a runway unless positive permission has been given and acknowledged.
A runway vacated report should not be made until the vehicle (and tow) is clear of the designated runway area.
When an ATS Unit issues an instruction to cross a runway, the appropriate holding point designator shall be included in the instruction.
A vehicle driver should query any instruction that identifies a holding point designator inconsistent with the vehicle location, or the driver’s request, before proceeding onto the runway.
Where it is not possible for the controller to issue permission to cross the runway, alternative instructions may be given.
Positive permission must be given and acknowledged before a vehicle driver enters a runway to carry out a specialised task.
If a vehicle is operating on the runway, it will be instructed to vacate the runway when it is expected that an aircraft will be landing or taking off.
When a vehicle is moving on the movement area it may be necessary to inform the vehicle of a potentially dangerous situation and to tell it to stop.
Drivers of vehicles required to tow aircraft should state the type, and where applicable the operator, of the aircraft to be towed in the first call.
Where it is necessary for the tug to push an aircraft back from a parking standing before towing, this should be included.
Arrangements for notifying low visibility procedures vary between aerodromes and may include a broadcast by the controller.
Information regarding the safety of a specific aircraft should be transmitted to the controller/FISO.
Drivers should follow the procedures for their particular aerodrome when reporting sightings of wildlife.
If a driver is lost or unsure of the vehicle’s location he should inform the controller/FISO immediately and follow instructions.

The driver of a broken-down vehicle should inform the controller/FISO immediately, including precise information regarding the vehicle’s location and follow the aerodrome’s procedures for broken-down vehicles.
In the event of a radio failure, drivers should follow the procedures for their aerodrome and comply with any light signals by the controller/FISO.
Controllers are not to instruct aircraft or vehicles to cross illuminated red stop-bars used at runway and intermediate taxiway holding positions.
The aerodrome operator may decide, on the grounds of safety, that inoperable stop-bars and associated taxiways be withdrawn from service and alternative routes used where practicable.
Under exceptional circumstances, when withdrawal of inoperable stop-bars is not possible and they cannot be readily suppressed, an aircraft may be instructed to cross such an illuminated stop-bar.
Clearance to cross a runway in use should normally be withheld until no confliction exists.

Clearance to cross a runway in use may be given subject to aircraft which are landing or taking off, provided the conditional clearance contains sufficient information to identify the other traffic and is related to one movement only.
When a clearance to cross a runway in use is issued, a report vacated instruction shall be included, unless the controller has continuous sight of the aircraft or vehicle crossing.
When passing taxi instructions that will position an aircraft to cross a runway, the controller may optionally insert the phrase 'hold short of' prior to the runway designator.
Messages shall not be transmitted to an aircraft during take-off, the last part of final approach or the landing roll, unless necessary for safety reasons.
Radio operators must use the full callsign, including the suffix 'RADIO', in response to the initial call from an aircraft and on any other occasion that there is doubt.
Air traffic controllers providing an Air/Ground Communication Service must be careful not to lapse into providing an air traffic control service.

Personnel providing an Air/Ground Communication Service must ensure that they do not pass a message which could be construed to be either an air traffic control instruction or an instruction issued by FISOs for specific situations.
When relaying clearances initiated by an air traffic control unit, the name of the authority must be included in the message.

Air Traffic Control clearances passed to radio operators to be issued on behalf of the ATC unit are to be read back in full to the issuing authority, and the pilot is to read back in full the clearance relayed by the Air/Ground Communicatio
The safe conduct of the flight remains the pilot’s responsibility, even when using information provided by an AGCS radio station operator.
Air ground operators must not use the expression 'at your discretion' as this is associated with the service provided by FISOs and is likely to cause confusion to pilots.
Response to an aircraft requesting joining information for a landing shall include runway designation, circuit direction, surface wind, QFE/QNH, and traffic information.
Response to an aircraft reporting joining the circuit shall be 'Roger' plus, when applicable, updated traffic information and any changes to aerodrome information.
Response to an aircraft reporting landed and/or runway vacated shall include any appropriate aerodrome information.
Aeronautical radio stations located offshore on rigs, platforms and vessels provide an air-ground service to helicopters operating in the vicinity.
Offshore radio stations must identify themselves using the callsign specified by the CAA in the approval document.
No suffix will be added to the CAA approved callsign when traffic information is to be passed by the operator of the aeronautical radio station.
When logistics information is to be passed the suffix ‘LOG’ shall be added to the approved callsign.
Offshore station shall transmit 'Take the Flight Watch'; helicopter shall respond 'I have the Flight Watch'.
Offshore station shall transmit 'position …'; helicopter shall respond 'Roger'.
Offshore station shall transmit 'Report your weather'; helicopter shall respond with Surface Wind, Visibility, Weather, Cloud, Temperature, QNH/QFE, and Helideck status.
Offshore station shall transmit 'Switch on the NDB'; helicopter shall respond 'Wilco NDB frequency (number) kHz ident (letters) (if requested)'.
Helicopter shall transmit 'ETA is (time)'; offshore station shall respond 'Roger'.
Helicopter shall transmit 'Landing in (number) minutes'; offshore station shall respond 'Roger'.
The aircraft shall query deck availability using the phrase 'Is the deck available for landing?'
The offshore station shall respond with 'Affirm Deck available (for landing)', 'Deck obstructed, expect (number) minutes delay', or 'Deck closed due to (reason), expect (number) minutes delay'.
Transmission of the phrase 'for landing' in the deck availability response is optional.
When departing using an NDB, the aircraft shall report '[navigation aid designator] outbound'.
When requested by a vessel, the aircraft shall report its position using the phrase 'Position (lat/long)'.
When requested by a vessel, the aircraft shall report its course and speed using the phrase 'Course and speed (number) degrees (number) knots'.
When requested by a vessel, the aircraft shall report relative wind using the phrase 'Relative wind'.
When instructed by a vessel to maintain course and speed, the aircraft shall acknowledge with 'Roger'.
When instructed by a vessel to alter course, the aircraft shall acknowledge with 'Standby. Course now (number) degrees'.
When instructed by a vessel to change speed, the aircraft shall acknowledge with 'Standby. Speed now (number) knots'.
For operational purposes, 'Deck available (for landing)' should be considered to have the same meaning as 'Deck is clear for landing'.
Procedures for messages such as flight notification when no ATSU is present should be contained in the aircraft operator’s standard operating procedures.
Helicopter crews must be provided with accurate information regarding the pitch, roll and heave of the helideck.

Reports on pitch and roll should include values in degrees about both axes of the true vertical datum and be expressed in relation to the vessel’s heading, with pitch expressed as 'up'/'down' and roll as 'left'/'right'.
Heave should be reported in a single figure, being the total heave motion of the helideck rounded up to the nearest metre.
Heave is taken to be the vertical difference between the highest and lowest points of the helideck movement.
A standard radio message should be passed to the pilot containing the information on the helideck movement in an unambiguous format.
An example of the ‘standard message’ would be: ‘(Pitch, roll and heave). Roll one degree left and three degrees right; pitch two degrees up and two degrees down; heave two metres’.
Where an aeronautical communications frequency is allocated for use at a United Kingdom aerodrome, all RTF communications are to be conducted on the allocated frequency.
A common frequency (135.475 MHz) known as ‘SAFETYCOM’ is made available for use at aerodromes where no other frequency is allocated to enable pilots to broadcast their intentions.
Pilots should broadcast information on their intentions to other aircraft that may be operating on, or in the vicinity, of the aerodrome.
The phraseology to be used at an unattended aerodrome, as described in this section, is not to be used at aerodromes with ATS in attendance.
All transmissions at unattended aerodromes shall be addressed to ‘(Aerodrome name) Traffic’.
No reply to an unattended aerodrome report shall be transmitted.
Pilots should refer to the UK AIP to establish the joining and circuit procedure to be followed at specific aerodromes.
If a pilot elects to make unattended aerodrome reports, all those reports not listed as ‘optional’ should be included.
Pilots must maintain traffic awareness and lookout even when making unattended aerodrome reports, as monitoring is not a substitute for visual observation.
Transmission of unattended aerodrome reports does not confer any right-of-way.
Pilots shall comply at all times with the Rules of the Air Regulations, in particular the rules for avoiding aerial collisions.
SAFETYCOM is not an Air Traffic Service and no aeronautical ground station is associated with SAFETYCOM.
When using SAFETYCOM, RTF transmissions must identify the aerodrome name suffixed ‘traffic’.
SAFETYCOM transmissions must be correct and concise.

SAFETYCOM transmissions shall only be made when aircraft are not more than 2000 ft above aerodrome level, or not more than 1000 ft above promulgated circuit height (if applicable) and within 10 NM of the aerodrome of intended landing.
Where an aerodrome lies within controlled airspace, pilots are to call the appropriate ATSU and ensure that they obtain clearance to enter the airspace.
A taxiing transmission is optional and may be advisable at airfields where the view from an aircraft either in the air or on the ground may be restricted.
A reporting in the circuit transmission is optional and may be advisable depending on other traffic in the vicinity.
Standard meteorological abbreviations and terms should be used and the information should be transmitted slowly and enunciated clearly.
VOLMET callsign, frequency, operating hours, aerodromes, and contents are published in the UK AIP.
A VOLMET broadcast shall include Aerodrome identification, Surface wind, Visibility, RVR (if applicable), Weather, Cloud, Temperature, Dewpoint, QNH, and Trend (if applicable).
All VOLMET broadcasts are in English.
Numerals on essential words such as 'surface wind', 'visibility' etc. are not spoken.
‘SNOCLO’ is used to indicate that aerodrome is unusable for take-off/landings due to heavy snow on runways or snow clearance.
When transmitting the runway visual range the abbreviation RVR shall be used without using the phonetic word for each letter.
The runway designator may be omitted if there is no possibility of confusion.

Where instrumented RVR (IRVR) is not available, RVR for the purposes of Category 1 and non-precision instrument approach operations may be assessed by human observer and transmitted by the controller to the pilot.
If the assessed value is more than the maximum reportable value, controllers are to advise the pilot.
Where an ATIS broadcast is established, the controller does not need to pass departure information to the pilot when giving taxi instructions.
The controller must check that the aircraft is in possession of the latest QNH when ATIS is established.
Phraseology employed during pre-departure manoeuvres must not be interpretable as a take-off clearance or instruction to enter the runway.
Any instruction to use a runway shall include the designator of the runway.
When passing a take-off clearance, the runway designator should be stated first.
At busy aerodromes with separate ground and tower functions, aircraft are usually transferred to the tower frequency at or approaching the holding point.
Where appropriate, the controller should include the reason for a hold instruction at a specified holding point.
Many types of aircraft carry out engine checks prior to departure and are not always ready for take-off when they reach the holding point.
Air Traffic controllers may ask if a pilot can accept an intersection departure.
A pilot may request an intersection departure.
If no lights are visible controllers are to state “RVR less than (number) metres, inserting the value corresponding to one light.
Under no circumstances is a controller to pass a pilot information which suggests that the visibility is better than the RVR reported.

When a pilot’s report or an observation from the tower indicates a worse condition on the runway this information is to be passed to the pilot with subsequent RVR reports for as long as the condition is considered to exist.
Where RVR is not available the pilot is to be advised.
Where instrumented runway visual range (IRVR) observations are available, more than one reading may be transmitted.
When conditions of standing water, with or without reports of braking action, are brought to the attention of ATS, the available information will be passed to aircraft likely to be affected.

When reports are based on inspections of the runway surface made by the aerodrome authority, the presence or otherwise of surface water on a runway will be assessed over the most significant portion of the runway.
The presence or otherwise of surface water on a runway is reported in RTF and ATIS broadcasts using the following descriptions:
DRY: The surface is not affected by water, slush, snow, or ice.
Reports that the runway is dry are not normally to be passed to pilots. If no runway surface report is passed, pilots should assume the surface to be dry.
DAMP: The surface shows a change of colour due to moisture.
If there is sufficient moisture to produce a surface film or the surface appears reflective, the runway will be reported as WET.
WET: The surface is soaked but no significant patches of standing water are visible.
Standing water is considered to exist when water on the runway surface is deeper than 3mm. Patches of standing water covering more than 25% of the assessed area will be reported as WATER PATCHES.
WATER PATCHES: Significant patches of standing water are visible.
FLOODED: Extensive patches of standing water are visible.

Water patches will be reported when more than 25% of the assessed area is covered by water more than 3mm deep. Flooded will be reported when more than 50% of the assessed area is covered by water more than 3mm deep.

Reports originated by the Aerodrome Authority regarding runway surface conditions must be based on runway inspections and include the conditions in each third of the assessed area, sequentially, for the runway to be used.
Additional information indicating runway surface water conditions greater than assessed must be prefixed by the words 'Unofficial observation'.
When providing unofficial runway surface observations, the surface conditions must be advised using a single term for the entire runway.
When suitable equipment is available, reports of braking action on wet runways must be passed to pilots.
Other runway surface conditions, which may be of concern to a pilot, must be passed by ATS.
Pilots inbound to airports with ATIS are normally required to acknowledge receipt of current information on first contact with the aerodrome ATSU by quoting the code letter of the broadcast.
Pilots of outbound aircraft are not normally required to acknowledge receipt of departure ATIS except when requested on the actual ATIS broadcast.
If pilots report receipt of a departure ATIS broadcast, the QNH should be included to allow ATC to check that the quoted QNH is up-to-the-minute.
ATIS broadcasts should be no more than thirty seconds duration.
ATIS broadcasts will include all or part of the elements of the information shown in Appendix A to COM05: ICAO Annex 11 ATIS message elements.
A Trend may be included in an ATIS broadcast.
In rapidly changing meteorological situations where weather reports are impractical for ATIS, ATIS messages will indicate that weather information will be passed on RTF.
Any significant change to the content of a current ATIS message will be passed to pilots by RTF until such time as a new message is broadcast.
Messages shall not be transmitted to an aircraft during take-off, the last part of final approach or the landing roll, unless necessary for safety reasons.
At Position 1, the aircraft reports 'Downwind' leg.
At Position 2, the aircraft reports 'Late downwind' if it is on the downwind leg, has been unable to report 'Downwind' and has passed the downwind end of the runway.
At Position 3, the aircraft reports 'Base' leg (if required).
At Position 4, the aircraft reports 'Final' and clearance to land is issued here.
At Position 5, the aircraft reports 'Long final' (between 8 and 4 miles) when aircraft is on a straight in approach.
For light aircraft operations, circuit dimensions may be reduced but the relative RTF reporting points are maintained.
Details of military visual circuit patterns are found in Chapter 11.
When line-up will take place at a position other than for a full-length runway departure the intermediate ‘Holding Point’ designator shall be included in the line-up instruction.
Controllers may include the runway ‘Holding Point’ designator in any other line-up instruction when considered necessary.
Information on the Take-Off Run Available (TORA) from the intersection shall be issued when requested by a pilot or whenever deemed necessary by the controller.
The term Take-Off Run Available (TORA) shall be pronounced TORAH.
For reason of expedition, a controller may wish to line-up an aircraft for departure before conditions allow take-off.

Phraseology for line-up and wait with one aircraft to depart before you from a holding point: '[Callsign], via [holding point] line-up and wait [runway], one aircraft to depart before you from [holding point]'.
Phraseology for line-up and wait as number two for departure: 'Via [holding point] line-up and wait [runway], number two for departure, [Callsign]'.
Except in cases of emergency, messages will not be transmitted to an aircraft in the process of taking off or in the final stages of an approach and landing.
Controllers shall use the phraseology 'G-CD, cleared for take-off' or 'Cleared for take-off, G-CD' for take-off clearances.
The surface wind will be passed if there is a significant difference to that already passed.
The averaging period for wind observations is two minutes for reports used at an aerodrome for take-off and landing and for wind indicators in air traffic service units.

The instantaneous surface wind should be available to be given to pilots on request particularly at aerodromes supporting primarily the operations of aircraft whose maximum total weight authorised is 5,700 kg or less.
When a pilot requests the instantaneous surface wind, the word 'instant' is to be inserted to indicate that the wind being reported is not the two minute average.
A take-off clearance shall be issued separately from any other clearance message.
When cleared for immediate take-off and at the holding point, the pilot must taxi immediately onto the runway and commence take-off without stopping the aircraft.
When cleared for immediate take-off and already lined up on the runway, the pilot must take off without delay.
If an immediate take-off is not possible while lined up on the runway, the pilot must advise the controller.
A controller may line up an aircraft for departure before conditions allow take-off for reasons of expedition.
Phraseology for immediate takeoff clearance includes the runway designation, the instruction 'cleared for immediate take-off', and the aircraft callsign.
Phraseology for 'line-up and wait' includes the instruction 'line-up and wait', the runway designation, and the aircraft callsign.
Phraseology for takeoff clearance includes the runway designation, the instruction 'cleared for take-off', and the aircraft callsign.
In poor visibility the controller may prefix the clearance with the runway designator and request the pilot to report when airborne.
Runway 28 cleared for take-off. Wilco, BIGJET 347
BIGJET 347, runway 28 cleared for take-off report airborne
BIGJET 347, airborne
BIGJET 347, contact Radar 121.750
Radar 121.750, BIGJET 347
Conditional clearances are only to be provided subject to conditions specified by the relevant authority.
Military controllers do not apply conditional clearances.
Conditional phrases will not be used for movements affecting the active runway(s), except when the aircraft or vehicles concerned are seen by the controller and pilot.
Conditional clearances are to relate to one movement only and, in the case of landing traffic, this must be the first aircraft on approach.
A conditional instruction shall include the callsign.
A conditional instruction shall include the condition.
A conditional instruction shall include identification of the subject of the condition.
A conditional instruction shall include the clearance.
A conditional instruction shall include reiteration of the condition.

If a conditional clearance has been issued in respect of a landing aircraft the stop-bar must not be deselected until the landing aircraft has passed the position at which the vehicle or aircraft will enter the runway.

For aircraft departing from the same runway holding position, when a conditional line-up clearance has been issued to a succeeding departing aircraft, the illuminated red stop-bar may remain deselected provided that it will be the next move
Any instruction to use a runway shall include the designator of the runway.
When passing the clearance, the runway designator should be stated first.

An Omnidirectional Departure procedure is designed on the basis that an aircraft maintains runway direction until it reaches such a height that it can make a turn in any direction and maintain the prescribed obstacle clearance.
Local departure instructions may be given prior to the take-off clearance to ensure separation between aircraft operating in the vicinity of the aerodrome.
Revised clearances and post departure instructions for aircraft on the runway or at the holding position shall be prefixed with an instruction to hold position.
When it is necessary to rescind the take-off clearance or quickly free the runway for landing traffic, the aircraft will be instructed to cancel take-off or stop immediately.
Instructions to cancel take-off or stop immediately must be repeated.
When a pilot abandons take-off, he should, as soon as practicable, inform the tower that he is doing so.
When a pilot abandons take-off, he should, as soon as practicable, inform the tower of the reasons for abandoning take-off if applicable, and request further manoeuvring instructions.
Requests for circuit-joining instructions should be made in sufficient time for a planned entry into the circuit taking other traffic into account.
Where ATIS is established, receipt of the broadcast should be acknowledged in the initial call to an aerodrome.
When the traffic circuit is a right-hand pattern it shall be specified.
A left-hand pattern need not be specified although it is essential to do so when the circuit direction is variable.
In some circumstances, an aircraft may be instructed to complete a standard overhead join.
Military procedures for cancelled take-offs appear in Chapter 10.
Depending on prevailing traffic conditions and the direction from which an aircraft is arriving, it may be possible to make a straight-in approach.

ATS personnel shall take into consideration the prevailing visibility, traffic situation, local procedures and the type of join being conducted to determine the timing and content of traffic information.
Pilots shall receive traffic information prior to joining the traffic circuit.
The pilot having joined the traffic circuit shall make routine reports as required by local procedures.
Where necessary, the controller may instruct the pilot to report at a specified position.
It may be necessary in order to co-ordinate traffic in the circuit, to issue a pilot his number in the sequence along with the position of the preceding aircraft and delaying action if necessary.
Aircraft shall overfly at 2000 ft above Aerodrome Elevation.
Pilots shall determine the circuit direction from signals, other traffic, or windsock if not already known.
Pilots shall descend on the 'dead side' to circuit height.
Pilots shall join the circuit by crossing the upwind end of the runway at circuit height.
Pilots shall position downwind.
Pilots should check beforehand whether specific joining procedures apply; otherwise the overhead join is the preferred method.
The first radio call should be made 5 - 10 miles from the aerodrome and joining checks completed.
Pilots shall maintain 2000ft above aerodrome elevation or 1000ft above promulgated circuit level (based on QNH from the nearest available source).
Pilots shall report OVERHEAD and include the appropriate runway if determined.
If unable to ascertain the runway in use, pilots shall continue circling overhead.
Pilots shall begin letting down on the dead side and report DEAD SIDE DESCENDING if required.
Once the circuit direction has been established, all turns must be in the circuit direction.
Pilots shall position to cross within the upwind threshold at circuit height.
Pilots should watch for aircraft taking off, as they could pose a hazard.
Pilots should watch for existing circuit traffic and adjust their path to sequence safely.
Pilots shall call downwind.
Pilots may make an optional call BASE LEG if required.
Pilots shall report FINAL.
A 'touch and go' is defined as the aircraft landing, continuing rolling, and taking off without stopping.
It is helpful for circuit management purposes if a controller is informed when an aircraft engaged in multiple approaches is on his last circuit.
A 'final' report is made when an aircraft has turned onto final approach.
If the turn on to final is made at a distance greater than 4 NM from touchdown, a 'long final' report is made.
The landing/touch and go/low approach clearance will include the runway designation.
Where established, an 'outer marker' instead of a 'final' report may be made.
Where a controller cancels a landing clearance but intends to re-issue it in good time, he should, if time permits, give the reason for cancelling the landing clearance.
If available, the instantaneous surface wind should be provided to the pilot on request.
If the runway is obstructed at the time of the 'final' report (at 4 NM or less) but is expected to be available in good time, the controller will delay landing clearance.
The instruction to 'continue' IS NOT an invitation to land and the pilot must wait for landing clearance or initiate a missed approach.

A landing aircraft may be permitted to touch down before a preceding landing aircraft has vacated the runway provided: 1. the runway is long enough to allow safe separation and braking is not adversely affected; 2. it is during daylight hou
A pilot may request to fly past the control tower or other observation point for the purpose of visual inspection from the ground.
If the low pass is made for the purpose of observing the undercarriage, 'landing gear appears down' may be used to describe its condition.
If the low pass is made for the purpose of observing the undercarriage, 'right (or left, or nose) wheel appears up (or down)' may be used to describe its condition.
If the low pass is made for the purpose of observing the undercarriage, 'wheels appear up' may be used to describe its condition.
If the low pass is made for the purpose of observing the undercarriage, 'right (or left, or nose) wheel does not appear up (or down)' may be used to describe its condition.
A pilot may request permission to make a low approach along the runway, without intending to land.
If the runway in use is occupied by aircraft or vehicles, an approaching aircraft may be cleared to carry out a low approach which includes a descent not below a specified height or altitude.
The minimum height or altitude is defined in regulatory documentation and/or local instructions as appropriate.
In such circumstances, the pilot is to be informed of the aircraft or vehicles on the runway.
Instructions to carry out a missed approach may be given to avert an unsafe situation.
Any transmissions to aircraft going around shall be brief and kept to a minimum.
An aircraft on an instrument approach is to carry out the published missed approach procedure.
An aircraft operating VFR is to continue into the normal traffic circuit unless instructions are issued to the contrary.
In the event of missed approach being initiated by the pilot, the phrase ‘going around’ shall be used.
Unless absolutely necessary, controllers will not give taxi instructions to pilots until the landing roll is complete.
Unless otherwise advised, pilots should remain on tower frequency until the runway is vacated.
The type of service provided at an aerodrome falls into one of three categories; examples in this section are confined to those used by air traffic controllers.
Phraseology used by FISOs and Air/Ground Communication Service operators is different from that used by controllers; examples are found in Chapter 4.
Where no ATIS is provided, the pilot may ask for current aerodrome information before requesting start up.
Phraseology for requesting departure information: 'Stourton Ground, [callsign], request departure information'.

Phraseology for providing departure information: '[Callsign], [Aerodrome], departure runway [n] wind [dir] [speed], QNH [n], temperature [n], dewpoint [n], RVR [n] [n] [n] metres. Runway [n], QNH [n], will call for start up, [Callsign]'.
Requests to start engines are normally made to facilitate ATC planning and to avoid excessive fuel wastage by aircraft delayed on the ground.
At certain aerodromes, along with the request, the pilot will state the location of the aircraft and acknowledge receipt of the departure ATIS broadcast identifying letter together with the QNH.
Phraseology for requesting start up with ATIS/QNH: '[Aerodrome] Ground, [Callsign], [stand] [information] [letter], QNH [n] request start up'.
When there will be a delay to the departure of the aircraft the controller will normally indicate a time to start up or expect to start up.
Phraseology for requesting start up: '[Aerodrome] Ground, [Callsign], information [letter] QNH [n], request start up'.
Phraseology for approving start up: '[Callsign], [Aerodrome] Ground, start up approved'.
Phraseology for indicating expected start up time: '[Callsign], [Aerodrome] Ground, expect start up at time [n]'.
Phraseology for indicating expected departure time and start up at own discretion: '[Callsign], [Aerodrome] Ground, expect departure at time [n] start up at own discretion'.
Essential Aerodrome Information is passed to aircraft whenever possible prior to start-up or taxi and prior to the commencement of final approach.
Messages will not be transmitted to an aircraft during take-off, the last part of final approach or the landing roll, unless it is necessary for safety reasons.
Generally, the AFISO is not permitted to issue instructions or advice to pilots of his own volition.
Elsewhere on the manoeuvring area and at all times in the air, information only shall be passed to pilots.
When passing messages on behalf of other agencies, AFISOs shall include the name of the agency so that pilots will be aware that the message comes from a legitimate source.
AFISOs must ensure that the information given to pilots is distinct and unambiguous.
An AFISO may request pilots to make position reports; these requests do not have the status of instructions.
AFISOs are not permitted to refuse entry into the ATZ when requested by a pilot.

Messages regarding a decision by the aerodrome authority not to permit an aircraft to land must be prefixed: 'Message from the aerodrome authority...' and may not be issued by AFISOs of their own volition.
RTF messages transmitted on aviation VHF frequencies should normally comprise callsign and text as described earlier in this document.
All phraseology shall be used in conjunction with callsigns (aircraft, ground vehicle, FIS or other) as appropriate.
The operative word in ground movement instructions is 'taxi' for aircraft, 'proceed' for vehicles, and 'tow' for tractors towing aircraft.
The text of messages should be composed from standard speech abbreviations and the standard phrases listed on the following pages.
One or more phrases may be used but all items in a phrase are to be included.
Words in parentheses indicate that specific information, such as a level, a place or a time, etc., must be inserted to complete the phrase, or alternatively that optional phrases may be used.
Words in square parentheses indicate optional additional words or information that may be necessary in specific instances.
Traffic information may use the phrase 'TRAFFIC (information);'.
Traffic information may use the phrase 'NO REPORTED TRAFFIC;'.
Traffic information may use the phrase '[FURTHER] TRAFFIC (direction) BOUND (type of aircraft) (level) ESTIMATED (or OVER) (significant point) AT (time);'.

Traffic information may use the phrase 'TRAFFIC IS (classification) UNMANNED FREE BALLOON(S) WAS [or ESTIMATED] OVER (place) AT (time) REPORTED (level(s)) [or LEVEL UNKNOWN] MOVING (direction) (other pertinent information, if any).'
Surface or instant wind shall be reported using the phraseology: [SURFACE] or [INSTANT] WIND (direction and speed) [(units)]; WIND AT (level) (number) DEGREES (number) KNOTS;
Wind is always expressed by giving the mean direction and speed and any significant variations thereof.
Visibility shall be reported using the phraseology: VISIBILITY (distance) (units) [direction];
Present weather shall be reported using the phraseology: PRESENT WEATHER (details);
Cloud shall be reported using the phraseology: CLOUD (amount, [(type)] and height of base) (units) (or SKY CLEAR);
CAVOK shall be reported using the phraseology: CAVOK;
CAVOK shall be pronounced CAV-O-KAY.
Temperature and/or Dewpoint shall be reported using the phraseology: TEMPERATURE [MINUS] (number) (and/or DEWPOINT [MINUS] (number));
QNH shall be reported using the phraseology: QNH (number) [Hectopascals];
QFE shall be reported using the phraseology: QFE (number) [Hectopascals].
For all transmissions, the word 'hectopascal' shall be appended to figures when transmitting a pressure setting below 1000 hPa, or in cases where confusion or ambiguity may result.
Windshear reports shall use the phraseology: AT (time) A DEPARTING/ARRIVING (a/c type) REPORTED WINDSHEAR AT (altitude). AIRSPEED LOSS/GAIN (number) KNOTS, STRONG LEFT/RIGHT DRIFT.
Phraseology for reporting passing a significant point shall be: REPORT PASSING (significant point).
Phraseology for reporting distance from a DME station or significant point shall be: REPORT (distance) MILES (GNSS or DME) FROM (name of DME station) (or significant point).
Phraseology for reporting passing a VOR radial shall be: REPORT PASSING (three digits) RADIAL (name of VOR) VOR.
Phraseology for reporting present position shall be: REPORT (GNSS or DME) DISTANCE FROM (significant point) or (name of DME station); or REPORT POSITION.
Phraseology for runway surface condition shall be: [(location)] RUNWAY SURFACE CONDITION RUNWAY (designator) (condition).
Phraseology for landing surface condition shall be: LANDING SURFACE (condition).
Phraseology for cautioning construction work shall be: CAUTION CONSTRUCTION WORK (location).
Phraseology for cautioning reasons on specific sides of a runway shall be: CAUTION (specify reasons) RIGHT (or LEFT), (or BOTH SIDES) OF RUNWAY [designator].

If considered appropriate, the pilot or ATSU may replace manufacturer’s name or aircraft model with the term ‘Helicopter’ where this may benefit the ATSU or other aircraft.

An instruction to ‘TAXI’ leaves the pilot free to select the most appropriate method, either ground taxi or air taxi.

If required and whenever possible, control instructions from the next ATS unit will be relayed until the pilot is able to change frequency.

Distress is defined as a condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and of requiring immediate assistance.
Urgency is defined as a condition concerning the safety of an aircraft or other vehicle, or of some person on board or within sight, but does not require immediate assistance.
For a Distress emergency, the pilot should start the emergency call with the international RTF prefix 'MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY'.
For an Urgency emergency, the pilot should start the emergency call with the international RTF prefix 'PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN'.
Pilots should address their emergency calls on 121.5 MHz or 243.0 MHz to ‘London Centre’.
Once two-way communication has been established, pilots should not leave 121.5 MHz or 243.0 MHz without telling the controller.
Pilots are urged to request assistance from the emergency service as soon as there is any doubt about the safe conduct of their flight.
Pilots should pass clear details of difficulties and requirements using the international standard RTF prefix 'MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY' or 'PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN' as appropriate.
If a pilot considers the problem not to be as serious as first thought and priority attention is no longer required, the emergency condition may be cancelled at the pilot’s discretion.
If a pilot is already in communication with an ATSU before the emergency arises, assistance should be requested from the controller on the frequency in use.
Any SSR code setting previously assigned by ATC (other than Conspicuity Code 7000) may be retained at the discretion of either the pilot or the controller.
If the pilot is not in direct communication with an ATSU and the aircraft is equipped with an SSR transponder, it should be switched to Emergency Code 7700, with Mode C if available.
If no acknowledgement of the distress or urgency message is made by the station addressed by the aircraft, other stations shall render assistance.
The originator of messages addressed to an aircraft in distress or urgency condition shall restrict to the minimum the number and volume and content of such messages as required by the condition.

The emergency message shall include present or last known position, flight level/altitude, and heading.

The emergency message should include any other useful information such as endurance remaining, POB, aircraft colour/markings, or survival aids.

A PAN PAN MEDICAL message shall convey the number and type of medical transports.

To advise a controller that a pilot is abandoning an aircraft equipped with an ejection seat, the phrase '(Callsign), Ejecting' shall be used.

During communication difficulties, a pilot may use an SSR transponder to acknowledge or respond to messages by transmitting SSR Code changes or squawking 'Ident' as requested.

Pilots who are unsure of their position should state this and request a position fix or make a 'PAN' call, rather than requesting a training fix.
Any aeronautical station or aircraft knowing of an emergency incident may transmit a distress message whenever such action is necessary to obtain assistance for the aircraft or vessel in distress.
In such circumstances, it should be made clear that the aircraft transmitting is not itself in distress.
Transmissions from aircraft in distress have priority over all other transmissions.

When receiving a Radar Advisory Service, the pilot remains responsible for terrain avoidance.

A message consists of four parts: The Callup, The Reply, The Message and The Acknowledgment.
Numbers occurring as round figures (e.g., 65, 2000, 11000) shall be spoken using specific conventions: 65 is six-five, 2000 is two thousand, and 11000 is One One Thousand.

English must be used for air–ground communications unless an alternative has been arranged with ATC.
A continuous listening watch should be maintained at all times, especially when transiting controlled airspace during notified hours of watch.
Pilots must report their position and height on entering and just before leaving an ATZ.
The correct procedure for setting the Squelch is to rotate the knob until the hiss just stops and leave it there.
Pilots should wait a split second to speak after pressing the transmit button to allow system relays to switch over.
It is an offence to use a callsign for a purpose other than that for which it is notified.
Communications should be restricted to what is required for the task in hand, using concise and unambiguous phraseology to avoid RTF congestion.

If in doubt, clear the zone the most direct way as quickly as possible, avoiding airfields, and making blind transmissions.
If in a circuit and radio fails, repeatedly switch the landing lights on and off.
In the open FIR, with unlimited visibility and no cloud, land at the nearest suitable aerodrome and inform ATC.
Make reports at scheduled times or positions, preceded by the phrase 'Transmitting Blind due to receiver failure'.
A system of flying a left or right-handed triangle pattern can be used to be seen on radar during radio failure.

If able, squawk Mode C to provide a height readout.
If only receiving, fly in a right-handed pattern for a minute (two minutes if over 300 knots) at best endurance speed with tight 120-degree turns.
If unable to transmit or receive, go to the left.

For abnormal de/anti-icing operations involving nozzle proximity activation, ATC shall advise the aircraft using the phraseology: 'BE ADVISED NOZZLE PROXIMITY ACTIVATION ON (significant point on aircraft) [NO VISUAL DAMAGE or DAMAGE (descri

For emergency situations in the de-icing bay, ATC shall advise the aircraft using the phraseology: 'EMERGENCY IN DE-ICING BAY (de-icing bay number) [SHUT DOWN ENGINES or STANDBY OR FURTHER INSTRUCTIONS]'.
Upon concluding de-icing/anti-icing procedure, the pilot shall report 'DE-ICING ON (areas treated) COMPLETE' and advise when ready for information.
The pilot shall report the type of fluid used (Type I/II/III/IV) during de-icing/anti-icing procedures.
The pilot shall report the holdover time started at (time).
The pilot shall report the appropriate anti-icing code.
For a two-step de-icing/anti-icing operation, the pilot shall report 'FINAL STEP STARTED AT (time)'.
Upon de-icing/anti-icing complete, the pilot shall report 'POST DE-ICING CHECK COMPLETED'.
Upon de-icing/anti-icing complete, the pilot shall report 'PERSONNEL AND EQUIPMENT CLEAR OF AIRCRAFT'.
An anti-icing code example for a mixture of 75% Type II fluid and 25% water commencing at 13:35h is recorded as 'TYPE II/75 13:35'.
Ground shall transmit the phrase 'DE-ICING STARTS NOW' to initiate de-icing operations.
Prior to de/anti-icing, ground shall instruct the flight crew to confirm brakes are set and treatment is required.
Prior to de/anti-icing, ground shall instruct the flight crew to hold position and confirm the aircraft is configured.
The pilot shall affirm brakes set and request treatment/areas, then affirm aircraft configured and readiness for de-icing.

VFR departure route clearance phraseology shall use 'LEAVE CONTROL ZONE [NIGHT VFR] VIA [VFR] [ROUTE/SECTOR] (route description) AT (level) [OR ABOVE/OR BELOW)] [SQAWK (code)] [RIGHT/LEFT TURN AFTER DEPARTURE]'.

IFR departure route clearance phraseology shall use 'CLEARED TO (clearance limit) [VIA] (route description/SID designator) [CLIMB] LEVEL (number)/(number) FEET [QNH (number)] SQUAWK (code) [(slot)] [(additional instructions)]'.
Phraseology for being unable to issue a departure clearance shall use 'UNABLE TO ISSUE (designator) DEPARTURE (reasons)'.
Additional clearance phraseology shall use 'CLEARED TO (clearance limit) VIA (designation)'.

Visual departure phraseology shall use 'REQUEST VISUAL DEPARTURE [DIRECT] TO/UNTIL (navaid, waypoint, altitude)' or 'REQUEST VISUAL LEFT/RIGHT TURN [DIRECT/TO (navaid, waypoint)]' for requests, and 'VISUAL DEPARTURE RUNWAY (number) APPROVED
Phraseology for standard departures shall use '(standard departure name and number) DEPARTURE'.

Post-departure turn or climb instructions phraseology shall use 'AFTER DEPARTURE (instructions)', 'AFTER DEPARTURE FLY HEADING (three digits)', 'AFTER DEPARTURE TURN RIGHT/LEFT HEADING (three digits) TO (level) [TO INTERCEPT (track, route,
Clearance to enter runway phraseology shall use 'LINE UP RUNWAY (number) [AND WAIT] [DORT HALTEN]' or 'LINE UP RUNWAY (number) PREPARE/BE READY FOR IMMEDIATE DEPARTURE'.
Multiple line up phraseology shall use 'LINE UP AND WAIT RUNWAY (number) INTERSECTION (name of intersection) (essential local traffic information)'.
For detailed information about standard instrument departure route clearances, refer to Phraseologies 5.7.1.1.
Ground crew shall use '[ARE YOU] READY TO START UP' and flight crew shall reply with 'STARTING NUMBER (engine number(s))' during start-up.
Ground crew should follow the start-up exchange with a reply on the intercom or a distinct visual signal to indicate all is clear and start-up may proceed.
Unambiguous identification of the parties concerned is essential in any communications between ground crew and pilots.

Phraseology for pushback/powerback includes: '[ARE YOU] READY FOR PUSH BACK/POWER BACK', 'READY FOR PUSH BACK/POWER BACK', 'CONFIRM BRAKES RELEASED', 'BRAKES RELEASED', 'COMMENCING PUSH BACK/POWER BACK', 'PUSHBACK/POWER BACK COMPLETED', 'ST
The pushback exchange is followed by a visual signal to the pilot to indicate that disconnect is completed and all is clear for taxiing.
Aerodrome control towers shall provide the pilot with the correct time prior to taxiing for take-off, unless arrangements exist for the pilot to obtain it from other sources.
Time checks shall be given at least to the nearest minute.
Air traffic services units shall provide aircraft with the correct time on request.
A time check before take-off must be done via the air-approved GPS in the aircraft (corrected to UTC).
If a time check via air-approved GPS is not possible, the pilot must inform aerodrome control and ask for the correct time.
At aerodromes where departure information is broadcast on ATIS, the request for departure information is omitted.
Acknowledgement of receipt of ATIS information must be made by including the ATIS identifying letter in the request for start up (IFR) or for taxi (VFR).
At aerodromes where route clearances are delivered on a special frequency, the ATIS identifying letter has to be included in the request for the route clearance.
The phraseology for requesting a tow is: 'REQUEST TOW [(company name)] (A/C type) FROM (location) TO (location)'.
The phraseology for responding to a tow request includes: 'TOW APPROVED VIA (specific route to be followed)', 'HOLD POSITION', or 'STAND BY'.
The phraseology for requesting start up is: '[(A/C location)] REQUEST START UP, INFORMATION [IS] (ATIS identification)'.

The phraseology for responding to a start up request includes: 'ANLASSEN GENEHMIGT', 'STAND BY FÜR ANLASSEN (Begründung)', 'ANLASSEN NEGATIV (Begründung)', '[ERWARTEN SIE] ANLASSEN UM (Zeit)', '[ERWARTEN SIE ABFLUG UM (Zeit)] ANLASSEN', 'NA

ATC shall issue clearance for touch and go, low approach, or low pass using the phraseology: 'RUNWAY (number) CLEARED TOUCH AND GO/LOW APPROACH/LOW PASS', optionally including altitude restrictions and go around instructions.
ATC shall issue 'CLEARED BRAKE OFF' with optional instructions when clearing an aircraft to brake off.
ATC shall use 'ACKNOWLEDGE BY ROCKING WINGS' or 'ACKNOWLEDGE BY FLASHING LANDING LIGHTS' to request visual acknowledgment of identification.

ATC shall use specific phraseology for landing sequences, including 'NUMBER (number) BEHIND (type of A/C) (position) (level)', 'NUMBER (number) FOLLOW (A/C type and position)', 'CAUTION WAKE TURBULENCE', or 'MAINTAIN OWN SEPARATION'.
ATC shall issue landing clearance using 'RUNWAY (number) CLEARED TO LAND', optionally preceded by wind information, and may add 'MAKE FULL STOP' or 'MAKE SHORT/LONG LANDING'.
When reduced runway separation is used, ATC shall issue landing clearance with traffic information: '(traffic information) WIND (number) DEGREES (number) KNOTS RUNWAY (number) CLEARED TO LAND'.
For helicopters, ATC shall issue landing clearance to a runway or helipad using 'RUNWAY (number)/HELIPAD (location on aerodrome) CLEARED TO LAND'.
ATC may authorize a helicopter to land at its own discretion using the phrase 'LAND AT OWN DISCRETION'.
ATC may issue specific approach instructions to helicopters, including straight-in/circling approach, turns, arrival routes, hold short instructions, and cautions for obstacles or wake turbulence.
ATC shall issue missed approach instructions using 'GO AROUND [IMMEDIATELY] [(instructions)] (reason)' or 'CONTINUE VISUALLY OR GO AROUND [(missed approach instructions)]'.
ATC may verify missed approach status using 'ARE YOU GOING AROUND' or provide contingency instructions using 'IN CASE OF GO AROUND (instructions)'.
ATC may instruct a pilot to continue the approach while preparing for a possible missed approach using 'CONTINUE APPROACH [PREPARE FOR POSSIBLE GO AROUND]'.
Section 5.3.2.11 (Missed approach) phraseology is provided in English only.
The phraseology 'PUSHBACK/POWERBACK APPROVED' is used to grant pushback or powerback approval.
The phraseology 'NEGATIVE PUSH BACK/POWERBACK' is used to deny pushback or powerback approval.
The phraseology 'STAND BY' is used to instruct an aircraft to wait for further instructions regarding pushback.
The phraseology 'EXPECT (number) MINUTES DELAY [DUE (reason)]' is used to inform an aircraft of an expected delay for pushback.
The phraseology 'G: PUSHBACK AT OWN DISCRETION' is used to grant pushback approval allowing the pilot to decide when to start.
The phraseology 'A: PUSHBACK/POWERBACK COMPLETED' is used by the aircraft to confirm completion of pushback or powerback.
Aircraft shall use the phraseology [(A/C location)] REQUEST PUSHBACK/POWERBACK to request pushback or powerback.
ATC shall use the phraseology START UP APPROVED to grant start-up clearance.
ATC shall use the phraseology STAND BY FOR START UP (reason) to delay start-up.
ATC shall use the phraseology NEGATIVE START UP (reason) to deny start-up.
ATC shall use the phraseology [EXPECT] START UP AT (time)/IN (number) MINUTES to provide expected start-up time.
ATC shall use the phraseology [EXPECT DEPARTURE AT (time)/IN (number) MINUTES] START UP AT OWN DISCRETION to grant start-up at pilot's discretion.
Aircraft shall use the phraseology REPORT [WHEN] READY FOR START UP to indicate readiness for start-up.
Start-up communications between ground and cockpit shall be conducted in English.
The pilot shall use the phraseology '[(Flugzeugposition)] ERBITTE PUSHBACK/POWERBACK' to request pushback or powerback.
The ground controller shall use the phraseology 'PUSHBACK/POWERBACK GENEHMIGT' to approve a pushback or powerback request.
The ground controller shall use the phraseology 'NEGATIV PUSHBACK/POWERBACK' to deny a pushback or powerback request.
The ground controller shall use the phraseology 'STAND-BY' to instruct the pilot to wait during pushback/powerback procedures.
The ground controller shall use the phraseology 'ERWARTEN SIE (Minutenanzahl) VERZÖGERUNG [WEGEN (Grund)]' to inform the pilot of a delay duration and reason.
The ground controller shall use the phraseology 'PUSHBACK NACH EIGENEM ERMESSEN' to authorize the pilot to perform pushback at their own discretion.
The pilot shall use the phraseology 'PUSHBACK/POWERBACK BEENDET' to indicate that the pushback or powerback procedure is completed.
A pilot requesting departure from a runway intersection shall transmit: 'REQUEST DEPARTURE FROM RUNWAY (number) INTERSECTION (designation or name of intersection)'.
When approving an intersection takeoff, ATC shall transmit: 'APPROVED, TAXI TO HOLDING POINT RUNWAY (number) INTERSECTION (designation or name of intersection)'.
When denying an intersection takeoff, ATC shall transmit: 'NEGATIVE, TAXI TO HOLDING POINT RUNWAY (number), [INTERSECTION (designation or name of intersection)]'.
When asking if the pilot is able to depart from an intersection, ATC shall transmit: 'ADVISE IF ABLE TO DEPART FROM RUNWAY (number) INTERSECTION (designation or name of intersection)'.
When providing TORA for an intersection takeoff, ATC shall transmit: 'TORA RUNWAY (number) FROM INTERSECTION (designation or name of intersection), (distance) METRES'.
A takeoff clearance shall include wind information and runway number, followed by 'CLEARED FOR TAKE OFF' or 'IMMEDIATE TAKE OFF', and optionally '[REPORT AIRBORNE]'.

The term TAKE OFF shall only be used for transmission or cancellation of the take off clearance itself; in all other situations concerning the departure of an aircraft, the word DEPARTURE shall be used.
When a takeoff clearance has not been complied with, ATC shall transmit 'REPORT ROLLING' and the pilot shall respond 'ROLLING'.
When a takeoff clearance has not been complied with, ATC shall transmit 'TAKE OFF IMMEDIATELY OR VACATE RUNWAY [(instructions)]'.
When a takeoff clearance has not been complied with, ATC may transmit 'TAKE OFF IMMEDIATELY OR HOLD AT HOLDING POINT/SHORT OF RUNWAY'.
To cancel a takeoff clearance, ATC shall transmit: 'HOLD POSITION, CANCEL TAKE OFF, I SAY AGAIN CANCEL TAKE OFF (reasons)'.
To stop an aircraft after it has commenced takeoff roll, ATC shall transmit: 'STOP IMMEDIATELY [(repeat A/C call sign) STOP IMMEDIATELY]'.
HOLDING and STOPPING are the procedural responses to the cancellation of takeoff clearance (5.3.1.12.2) and stopping after commencement of roll (5.3.1.12.3).
When reduced runway separation is used, ATC shall transmit traffic information followed by 'RUNWAY (number) CLEARED FOR TAKE OFF'.
A helicopter pilot requesting departure instructions shall transmit: 'REQUEST DEPARTURE INSTRUCTIONS'.
A helicopter takeoff clearance shall include wind information and runway number, followed by 'CLEARED FOR TAKE OFF'.

When authorizing helicopter takeoff at own discretion, ATC shall transmit wind information and '[FROM (location) PRESENT POSITION/ TAXIWAY (designator)/ FINAL APPROACH AREA (number)] TAKE OFF AT OWN DISCRETION'.
In radiotelephony phraseologies, the expression 'holding point' is used to designate the runway-holding position.
Aircraft shall use standard phraseology to request taxi, including aircraft type, wake turbulence category (if HEAVY/SUPER), location, and destination/intentions.
Aircraft may request detailed taxi instructions using the phrase 'REQUEST DETAILED TAXI INSTRUCTIONS'.
ATC shall issue taxi instructions to a holding point using the phrase 'TAXI TO HOLDING POINT RUNWAY [number]', optionally including route, time, or 'HOLD SHORT OF' instructions.
ATC shall issue taxi/turn instructions specifying the taxiway number or direction (left/right/straight) using standard phraseology.
ATC shall issue taxi instructions via a specific route, taxiway, or runway using the phrase 'TAXI VIA [identifier]'.
ATC may issue taxi instructions with caution or expedite modifiers using the phrases 'TAXI WITH CAUTION' and 'EXPEDITE TAXI [(reason)]'.
Aircraft shall acknowledge expedite or slower taxi instructions using the phrases 'EXPEDITING' and 'SLOWING DOWN' respectively.
ATC shall issue taxi instructions to a stand or to follow a marshaller using standard phraseology.
Aircraft shall use standard phraseology to request hovering overhead a specific location.
ATC shall issue hovering overhead instructions using the phrase 'HOVER OVERHEAD (location)' or 'HOVERING OVERHEAD (location) APPROVED'.
ATC shall issue traffic information instructions using the phrase 'GIVE WAY TO (description and position of other traffic)'.

The procedure words ROGER and WILCO are insufficient acknowledgement for the instructions HOLD, HOLD POSITION, and HOLD SHORT OF (position); the acknowledgement shall be by the phraseology HOLDING or HOLDING SHORT, as appropriate.
If the control tower is unable to see the crossing aircraft (e.g. night, low visibility) the instruction should always be accompanied by a request to report when the aircraft has vacated the runway.
The term 'holding point' shall only be intended for runways and not for Intermediate Holding Positions (IHPs).
Helicopter air-taxing requests shall use 'REQUEST AIR-TAXING' with routing details, and responses shall use 'AIR-TAXI' with destination/routing details.
Backtrack requests shall use 'REQUEST BACKTRACK [RUNWAY (number)]' and responses shall use 'BACKTRACK [RUNWAY (number)] APPROVED' or 'BACKTRACK LINE UP RUNWAY (number)'.
Runway crossing requests shall use 'REQUEST CROSS RUNWAY (number)' and responses shall use 'CROSS RUNWAY (number) [REPORT VACATED]'.
Taxi clearances to Intermediate Holding Positions shall use 'TAXI TO (designator of IHP) [VIA (route)]'.
A distress message sent by an aircraft in distress shall be on the air-ground frequency in use at the time.
A distress message shall consist of as many as possible of the specified message elements, spoken distinctly and in the specified order if possible.
The distress message shall include the name of the ATS unit addressed, if time and circumstances permit.
The distress message shall include the identification of the aircraft.
The distress message shall include the nature of the distress condition.
The distress message shall include the intention of the pilot in command.
The distress message shall include the present position, level, and heading.
The distress message may be made on the emergency frequency 121.500 MHz or another aeronautical mobile frequency if considered necessary or desirable.
The distress message may be broadcast if time and circumstances render this course preferable.
The aircraft may use any means at its disposal to attract attention and make known its conditions, including activating the appropriate SSR mode and code.
The ATS unit addressed is normally that ATS unit communicating with the aircraft or in whose area of responsibility the aircraft is operating.
The ATS unit addressed by an aircraft in distress, or the first ATS unit acknowledging the distress message, shall immediately acknowledge the distress message.

The ATS unit addressed by an aircraft in distress, or the first ATS unit acknowledging the distress message, shall take control of the communications or specifically and clearly transfer that responsibility, advising the aircraft if a trans

The ATS unit addressed by an aircraft in distress, or the first ATS unit acknowledging the distress message, shall take immediate action to ensure that all necessary information is made available, as soon as possible, to the ATS unit concer

The ATS unit addressed by an aircraft in distress, or the first ATS unit acknowledging the distress message, shall take immediate action to ensure that all necessary information is made available, as soon as possible, to the aircraft operat

The ATS unit addressed by an aircraft in distress, or the first ATS unit acknowledging the distress message, shall warn other ATS units, as appropriate, in order to prevent the transfer of traffic to the frequency of the distress communicat

The requirement to inform the aircraft operator concerned does not have priority over any other action which involves the safety of the flight in distress, or of any other flight in the area, or which might affect the progress of expected f

The aircraft in distress, or the ATS unit in control of distress traffic, shall be permitted to impose silence, either on all stations of the mobile service in the area or on any station which interferes with the distress traffic.
Instructions to impose silence shall be addressed 'to all stations' or to one station only, according to the circumstances.
When imposing silence, the phrase 'STOP TRANSMITTING' shall be used.
When imposing silence, the radiotelephony distress signal 'MAYDAY' shall be used.
The use of the signals specified in 4.1.2.3.1 shall be reserved for the aircraft in distress and for the ATS unit controlling the distress traffic.
Distress communications have absolute priority over all other communications.
ATS units/aircraft aware of distress communications shall not transmit on the frequency concerned unless specific exceptions apply.
ATS units/aircraft aware of distress communications may transmit on the frequency concerned if the distress is cancelled or the distress traffic is terminated.
ATS units/aircraft aware of distress communications may transmit on the frequency concerned if all distress traffic has been transferred to other frequencies.
ATS units/aircraft aware of distress communications may transmit on the frequency concerned if the ATS unit controlling communications gives permission.
ATS units/aircraft aware of distress communications may transmit on the frequency concerned if it has itself to render assistance.

Any ATS unit/aircraft which has knowledge of distress traffic, and which cannot itself assist the aircraft in distress, shall nevertheless continue listening to such traffic until it is evident that assistance is being provided.
When an aircraft is no longer in distress, it shall transmit a message cancelling the distress condition.

When the ATS unit which has controlled the distress communication traffic becomes aware that the distress condition is ended, it shall take immediate action to ensure that this information is made available, as soon as possible, to the ATS

The distress communication and silence conditions shall be terminated by transmitting a message, including the words 'DISTRESS TRAFFIC ENDED', on the frequency or frequencies being used for the distress traffic.

The message terminating distress traffic shall be originated only by the ATS unit controlling the communications when, after the reception of the message prescribed in point 4.1.2.5.1, it is authorised to do so by the competent authority.
Distress is defined as a condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and of requiring immediate assistance.
Urgency is defined as a condition concerning the safety of an aircraft or other vehicle, or of some person on board or within sight, but which does not require immediate assistance.
The radiotelephony distress signal 'MAYDAY' and the radiotelephony urgency signal 'PAN PAN' shall be used at the commencement of the first distress and urgency communication respectively.
At the commencement of any subsequent communication in distress and urgency traffic, it shall be permissible to use the radiotelephony distress and urgency signals.
The originator of messages addressed to an aircraft in distress or urgency condition shall restrict to the minimum the number and volume and content of such messages as required by the condition.

If no acknowledgement of the distress or urgency message is made by the ATS unit addressed by the aircraft, other ATS units shall render assistance as prescribed in points 4.1.2.2. and 4.1.2.3. respectively.

Distress and urgency communication shall normally be maintained on the frequency on which such traffic was initiated until it is considered that better assistance can be provided by transferring that traffic to another frequency.
In cases of distress and urgency communications, in general, the transmissions by radiotelephony shall be made slowly and distinctly, each word being clearly pronounced to facilitate transcription.

Crews of IFR flights subject to permanent (M)SSR surveillance must transmit the designation of the ATS unit being called when changing frequency during flight, unless advised differently by ATC or relevant publications.

Crews of IFR flights subject to permanent (M)SSR surveillance must transmit the aircraft call sign and, if identified as heavy by the competent authority, the word 'HEAVY' or 'SUPER' when changing frequency during flight.

Crews of IFR flights subject to permanent (M)SSR surveillance must transmit the level, including passing and cleared levels if not maintaining the cleared level, when changing frequency during flight.
Crews of IFR flights subject to permanent (M)SSR surveillance must transmit the speed if assigned by ATC when changing frequency during flight.
Crews of IFR flights subject to permanent (M)SSR surveillance may transmit additional elements as required by the pilot or air traffic control when changing frequency during flight.
When it is certain that the station called will receive the call, the crew of an IFR aircraft may transmit the message without waiting for a reply from the station called.
Pilots shall provide level information at the nearest full 30 m or 100 ft as indicated on the pilot's altimeter.
Full radiotelephony call signs shall always be used when establishing communication.
When establishing communication, aircraft shall start their call by the designation of the station called, followed by the designation of the station calling.
The reply to the above calls shall use the call sign of the station calling, followed by the call sign of the station answering.
The reply to the above calls shall be considered an invitation to proceed with transmission by the station calling.
For transfers of communication within one ATS unit, the call sign of the ATS unit may be omitted.
Communications shall commence with a call and a reply when it is desired to establish contact.
When it is certain that the station called will receive the call, the calling station may transmit the message without waiting for a reply from the station called.
After a call has been made to the aeronautical station, a period of at least 10 seconds should elapse before a second call is made.
When a station is called but is uncertain of the identification of the calling station, it should reply by transmitting: STATION CALLING (station called) SAY AGAIN YOUR CALL SIGN.
When an aeronautical station is called simultaneously by several aircraft stations, the aeronautical station shall decide the order in which aircraft stations shall communicate.
When issuing ATC clearances and reading back such clearances, controllers and pilots shall always add the call sign of the aircraft to which the clearance applies.
For other than ATC clearance occasions, continuous two-way communication after contact has been established shall be permitted without further identification or call until termination of the contact.

The calling procedure of an aircraft station establishing communication shall include: Designation of the station called; Designation of the station calling; and, for aircraft in the heavy wake turbulence category, the word 'Heavy' or 'Supe
The reply to the above calls shall include: Call sign of the station called; Designation of the answering station.
Example of initial call: LINZ TOWER, OE-ABC
Example of reply: OE-ABC, LINZ TOWER

In order to avoid triggering the alerting service, an acknowledgement by WIEN INFORMATION should be awaited after 'LEAVING FREQUENCY' was announced.
